title: 5 Ways You're Telling Students You Can't
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that well-meaning teachers frequently and unknowingly send students the devastating message that they are not capable, through five specific practices: poor preparation for independent work that leaves students needing constant help; micromanaging tasks students could do alone, which stunts maturity; inconsistency in enforcing accountability, which implies certain students aren't worth the effort; placing students in separate reading or math groups, which labels them as lesser even when a disability diagnosis is legitimate; and grade inflation, which feels good in the short term but delays a painful reckoning until students face real-world demands they weren't actually prepared for. His central claim is that these practices are standard, institutionally sanctioned teaching behavior, yet each quietly communicates low expectations that students internalize and live down to. The prescribed alternative throughout is to raise the bar and take direct responsibility for closing gaps -- through detailed lessons, teaching up rather than grouping down, and honest grading -- rather than softening expectations.
points: If students need hand-holding during independent work, it's not the students' fault -- it's a sign they weren't prepared well enough beforehand.
Grouping students into separate 'special' reading or math groups labels them as lesser, even when a diagnosed learning disability is legitimate.
Grade inflation feels good short-term for everyone involved but delays a painful reckoning until college, standardized tests, or the job market.
Inconsistent accountability quietly tells struggling students they're a lost cause not worth the effort to correct.
The alternative to all five patterns is to raise expectations and take direct responsibility for teaching up, rather than accommodating down.
quotes: In ways subtle but clear, scores of teachers are communicating to their students every day that they can’t do it. They don’t measure up.
In fact, they believe they’re helpful and supportive. But for students, the message they actual receive is devastating. Some never recover.
Independent work is meant for mastering material already learned. It's not learning itself. If there is consistent daily uncertainty, you're telling your students that they're not good at learning.
Because it labels them as dumb. They know it and so does everyone else.
That child you gave a passing grade to who did not earn it, whose skills did not warrant it, will discover one day that you lied.
They can’t read or write, think or communicate, reason or discern well enough to compete in today’s world.
